When will I use this?

Averages and statistics: when will I use this?

Whenever one reading isn't enough to trust.

Practice nurse

Route: Health and science

Uses example figures: the numbers marked (example figure) or (example figures) are made up to show the method.

One blood pressure reading can mislead, so NICE says to take readings at home, twice a day for 4 to 7 days, ignore the first day, and use the mean of the rest. After day 1, the top (systolic) numbers are 138, 134, 136, 140, 132, 136 (example figures).

  1. Add them: 816.
  2. Mean: \(816 \div 6 = 136\).
  3. The doctor compares that average, with the clinic reading, against NICE's limits.

Health visitor

Route: Health and science

Babies' weights are plotted on growth charts with centile lines. A centile shows how many healthy children are expected to be below that line. A baby is on the 91st centile.

  1. 91 out of 100 healthy babies the same age are expected to weigh less.
  2. \(100 - 91 = 9\) out of 100 are expected to weigh more.

Ecologist

Route: Agriculture, environmental and animal care

Uses example figures: the numbers marked (example figure) or (example figures) are made up to show the method.

You can't count every wild orchid in a meadow, so ecologists count them in a few 1 m² squares (quadrats) placed at random, and scale up. Ten quadrats count 3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 4, 5, 2, 6 (example figures). The meadow is 1500 m².

  1. Total: 40. Mean: \(40 \div 10 = 4\) orchids per m².
  2. Estimate: \(4 \times 1500 = 6000\) orchids.

Meteorologist

Uses example figures: the numbers marked (example figure) or (example figures) are made up to show the method.

"Warmer than average" means compared with a 30-year average. The Met Office now uses 1991–2020.

  1. UK mean temperature, 1961–1990: 8.3 °C. 1991–2020: 9.1 °C.
  2. Change: \(9.1 - 8.3 = 0.8\) °C warmer.
  3. How a mean works: five Julys of 19.2, 20.1, 18.7, 21.3 and 19.7 °C (example figures) total 99.0; mean \(99.0 \div 5 = 19.8\) °C.

Practise it

Games on MaffsGames that practise averages and statistics:

  • Distinctly Average: Find the mean, median, mode and range of data sets, then frequency tables and missing values.
  • Chart Interrogator: Read stem and leaf, box plots, cumulative frequency and histograms, then compare data sets.
  • Stat Attack: Modal class, median class, estimated mean and standard deviation from grouped frequency tables.
  • I Found a Mark: Break big exam questions into steps and bank the method marks: choose the calculations a marker credits, never the answer.

Sources

Every job and every figure that is not an example comes from a public page you can check.

  • Practice nurse: NICE guideline NG136, Hypertension in adults
  • Health visitor: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, UK-WHO growth charts
  • Ecologist: Oak National Academy, "Estimating population size using quadrats"; Skills England occupational map (Ecologist)
  • Meteorologist: Met Office, climate averages notes; Met Office, "How have daily temperatures shifted in the UK's changing climate?"
